newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos touts total success for APEC, others moan.
newsitem.headline: Ramos touts total success for APEC, others moan.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday the Philippines sought total success for this year's Asia-Pacific summit to be attended by the leaders of the United States, China, Japan and other nations of the booming Pacific rim.

"We have done everything possible and we have assured the 18 member economies that everything is ready here," he told a news conference at the start of six days of meetings culminating in the summit on Monday at Subic Bay, the former giant U.S. naval base north of Manila.
"We want total success."

U.S. President Bill Clinton, China's Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and a host of other heads of state and government are coming to the Philippines to seal what officials predict will be a turning point for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) organisation in its drive to become the world's biggest free-trade bloc within a quarter century.

APEC, which began in 1989 as a ministerial meeting in Australia, has been dismissed by critics as nothing but a talking shop and the summit that has now become an annual rite as a mere photo opportunity.
But organisers say the Manila and Subic meetings will start to produce concrete progress towards APEC's goal of dropping all trade and investment barriers in the region by 2020.
Philippine officials say the leaders will consider expanding the 18-member grouping, with southeast Asian members lobbying hard for Vietnam to be the first new entrant.
"We want it as soon as possible -- no date would be soon enough," he said. "This week would be fine."
Malaysia said on Wednesday it would support Peru's bid to become a member.

Fearing protests by anti-APEC leftists decrying what they call a club for big business, the Philippines has imposed strict security measures for this fourth annual summit and the conference of foreign and economic ministers on Friday and Saturday.
It also banned a proposed visit by Nobel peace laureate and East Timor independence leader Jose Ramos-Horta, and warned foreigners against interfering in Philippine affairs.
Manila officials say the leftists are trying to stir up labour unrest and stage other protests to embarrass the government.

A security alert involving a pipe bomb briefly raised temperatures at Subic on Wednesday -- but it was only a drill, said Richard Gordon, chairman of the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority which is transforming the abandoned base into an industrial development zone.
The Philippines sees its role as APEC host as an opportunity to showcase its economic recovery and to shake off its old image as the sick man of Asia.
Ramos said he hoped APEC would show the world "we are attractive, we are competitive, we are capable and that we have a contribution to make... to the Asia-Pacific economies".
The summit also provides opportunities for face-to-face meetings between leaders. Among bilaterals already announced are between Clinton and Jiang and Clinton and Hashimoto.

One of the summit's other results is likely to be a united APEC front at next month's World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting over a U.S. proposal for liberalisation in the trade in information technology products, diplomats and officials said.

Clinton, visiting Australia on his way to the Philippines, urged fellow Asia-Pacific leaders on Wednesday to spearhead the free trade push with cuts to barriers in the $1 trillion-a-year information technology industry.
Despite the Philippine government's push for the Subic summit's success, APEC has not won the hearts and minds of all Filipinos.
The capital's normally impossible traffic has been made even worse by so-called "friendship lanes" from which vehicles without special passes are banished, infuriating other road-users.
Five Filipinos shaved their heads to demonstrate their opposition to the summit and 30 colleagues began a 24-hour fast.

"This is our way of showing what APEC will do to our country. Foreign companies will come and exploit our cheap labour and deplete our environment," housewife Jesusa Rebite, 30, told reporters while fellow demonstrators gave her and four male activists a crude shave with scissors and blades.
